20.history: The great river port of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the north-central country keeps the carved stone, which the town scrubbed of a century's coal-smoke for the midsummer fair in the seventh year, finding under the black a second band of carving no one living had seen. An siathamh rèisimeid was raised at Cnoc bheag in {{year:VI-0101}} to hold the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and Òrd an t-Seabhaig blessed its colours by their own rite; it drilled in the square beside the stone. It keeps the posts by the boundary stones where the Tuathaich going south show their passes. A hewer's son of the town beat An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man at Còmhrag Ceann leathan of the present year. Òrd an t-Seabhaig of the town keep their own rite, older than the regiment, and the regiment's colours hang in their hall between musters; the river port below the town is the busiest of the north-central country, and its quays take the dubhan for the northern road.
20.known_for: the carved stone and An siathamh rèisimeid

475.history: The river port of the north-east raised An ceathramh rèisimeid in {{year:VI-0103}}. It marched down to the river and went down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar in old coal barges fitted with plank benches, in a day and a half on a high river, to be shipped round the north coast to Ceann mhòr. It came home in {{year:VI-0142}} after four years in the Tuathaich north, and lies at Caol bheag. The regiment's barracks are the old wool stores by the river landing, and the town, which had seen the regiment go out in coal barges, saw it come home by the road in lorries, its colours cased. The maor gave a supper for the officers and none for the men, and the town gave one for the men.

143.history: The Tuathaich headland harbour under the Baile chrom light had one of the three northern dubhan depots from {{year:VI-0048}}, supplied by sea. An ceathramh rèisimeid was landed there in the first winter of the war from hired hulls and quartered in the old human magistrate's house, the maor giving up the greater part of it and moving his household into the two upper rooms. Tional nan Tuathach protested and was answered that the arrangement stood. Corporal Dùghall mac Iain was billeted on Barbara Keir, who would not give him her tongue, and heard the hymns through the wall; the regiment's files patrolled the Ceann mhòr road through the quartered year, and a byre-boy took to lifting a hand to them as they passed. When the regiment went home Tional nan Tuathach asked that the house be given to the town, and it was given to the maor.

103.history: The eastern town on the Abhainn chaol raised An t-ochdamh rèisimeid in {{year:VI-0106}} to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council feared the holdouts might fire. Its guard was made lasting in {{year:VI-0141}}; its officers took houses in the town in place of quarters borrowed from the tank-yard's sheds, and the house of Na Seann Spioradan at Inis uaine added the regiment to its prayers. The regiment keeps a school in its barracks for its children and the town's. The tank-yard of the eastern ports lies on the river below the town, the largest store of dubhan outside the southern works, and the regiment's sentries walk its fence day and night; no holdout came within a hundred miles of it.
103.known_for: An t-ochdamh rèisimeid's guard on the eastern tanks

170.history: The south-west anchorage of the wolf-post quays took up engines early: two of its skippers sent for burners and a boatwright of Caol fhiadhaich in the sixth year, and a dubhan pump was set on its quays in the fifteenth, the first on that coast. An treas cabhlach was raised there in {{year:VI-0107}} and took the quays for its own, the fishing boats going to the old beach with their pump; it carried the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills. The quays were lengthened by forty paces for its tank-hulls in {{year:VI-0135}}. The wolf-posts that gave the quays their name were cut down to make room for the tank-hulls' moorings, and one was kept, at the quay's end, for the town's sake.
170.known_for: An treas cabhlach's anchorage and tank-hulls

215.history: The fortified headland harbour at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm put out the hired dubhan hulls that carried An ceathramh rèisimeid round the north coast in the first winter of the war; rounding the north cape a boy of the regiment's second company went overboard reaching for a loose line and was hauled back half-drowned, and one hull, parted from the rest in the second night's weather, put into a cove beyond the cape and came in to Ceann mhòr three days behind the others with crew and cargo whole. The town is a fortified harbour of old walls on the headland, whose masters of hulls hire out tank-hulls to Comhairle nam Mèinnean and the fleets alike; its quay was the only one on the coast long enough for An ceathramh rèisimeid's whole embarkation in one tide, and its harbour-master entered the regiment in his book as freight.
215.known_for: the hired hulls of An ceathramh rèisimeid
